units.title: Before you believe it, verify it
units.objective: Distinguish what a source claims from what the available evidence actually verifies.
key_points: A plausible statement is not necessarily a verified fact.
A source can accurately be quoted while the underlying claim remains unverified.
Generative AI can sound confident without independently establishing the truth.
units.exercise: An online article states that a library opened in 1920. What can you establish after reading only that article?
units.suggested_answer: You can establish that the article makes the claim. You cannot yet establish the opening date without corroboration.

units.title: Facts, claims, sources and interpretations
units.objective: Separate four levels of information before reaching a conclusion.
key_points: Fact: an element supported by verifiable evidence.
Claim: what a person, document or system states.
Source: the identifiable origin of a claim.
Interpretation: meaning assigned to the available evidence. Break compound statements into independently checkable Minimal Verification Units (MVUs).
units.exercise: Someone says, 'I was in Rome that day.' Identify the claim and the source. What additional evidence might support the event?
units.suggested_answer: The sentence is a claim; the speaker is its source. Travel records or independent observations may help, but no single document necessarily settles the question.

units.title: How much can we actually assert?
units.objective: Calibrate conclusions to the strength of the evidence.
key_points: VERIFIED (CERTO): supported within the stated evidentiary context, not absolute truth.
REPORTED (RIPORTATO): a statement attributed to a specific source.
LIMIT (LIMITE): a point the evidence does not resolve.
Avoid overstating certainty, omitting limitations or merging categories.
units.exercise: An archive website states that a register records a castle's construction in 1427. You have read the website, but not the register. What is verified?
units.suggested_answer: It is verified that the website contains this statement. The register's content and the historical construction date require separate verification.

units.title: Not all sources carry equal weight
units.objective: Evaluate provenance, independence, directness and the limits of each source.
key_points: Identify who created each source, when, why and for whom.
Distinguish original records from summaries, quotations and reposts.
Two websites repeating one press release do not count as independent confirmation.
A source can be authentic but irrelevant to the specific claim.
units.exercise: Three blogs repeat the same unsourced sentence. How many independent confirmations do you have?
units.suggested_answer: None established. Repetition is not independence; trace the wording back to its origin.

units.title: When sources disagree
units.objective: Document conflicts instead of hiding them behind a smooth narrative.
key_points: Record each claim alongside its source and exact wording.
Check whether apparent conflicts involve different definitions or timeframes.
Preserve competing accounts when the evidence cannot decide between them.
Explain which facts remain supported and which questions stay open.
units.exercise: A diary dates an event to 12 May, but a letter written on 14 May describes it as upcoming. How should you report the date?
units.suggested_answer: Report the conflicting evidence with attribution and leave the precise date unresolved until further verification.

units.title: Applying the Bottino Method
units.objective: Create an auditable evidence trail from question to conclusion.
key_points: Define the question and divide it into verifiable claims or MVUs.
Record source, date accessed, quotation, evidence and classification.
Check provenance and independence before drafting.
Write a conclusion whose scope matches the documented evidence and limits.
units.exercise: Build a four-column log for a historical claim: claim, source, status and next verification step.
units.suggested_answer: Each claim needs a traceable source, a justified status and an explicit next step or documented limit.

units.title: Artificial intelligence under scrutiny
units.objective: Use AI as an aid without treating generated answers as verified sources.
key_points: Treat model output as a proposal requiring independent checks.
Verify references, document identifiers, quotations and dates at their actual source.
Do not infer a document's contents merely because a catalogue identifier exists.
Record how AI was used and where human verification was performed.
units.exercise: An AI supplies an archival reference. The reference exists, but the record has not been inspected. What is established?
units.suggested_answer: Only the existence of that reference in the catalogue. The claimed contents remain unverified.

units.title: Final case: a conflicting dossier
units.objective: Produce a defensible conclusion from incomplete and contradictory records.
key_points: A municipal resolution dated 6 April authorises work.
A newspaper dated 7 April states that work began 'yesterday'.
A later web summary gives 5 April as the start date, without a citation.
Separate authorisation from actual commencement and preserve the unresolved conflict.
units.exercise: Write a short conclusion that does not exceed the evidence.
units.suggested_answer: The resolution documents an authorisation dated 6 April. The newspaper and web summary give conflicting indications about when work actually began. The evidence described does not establish the start date.
